function.name: patch
function.description:
Targeted find-and-replace edits in files. Use this instead of sed/awk in terminal. Uses fuzzy matching (9 strategies) so minor whitespace/indentation differences won't break it. Returns a unified diff. Auto-runs syntax checks after editing.

REPLACE MODE (mode='replace', default): find a unique string and replace it. REQUIRED PARAMETERS: mode, path, old_string, new_string.
PATCH MODE (mode='patch'): apply V4A multi-file patches for bulk changes. REQUIRED PARAMETERS: mode, patch.

mode.description: Edit mode. 'replace' (default): requires path + old_string + new_string. 'patch': requires patch content only.

path.description: REQUIRED when mode='replace'. File path to edit.

old_string.description: REQUIRED when mode='replace'. Exact text to find and replace. Must be unique in the file unless replace_all=true. Include surrounding context lines to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: REQUIRED when mode='replace'. Replacement text. Pass empty string '' to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false)

patch.description:
REQUIRED when mode='patch'. V4A format patch content. Format:
*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: path/to/file
@@ context hint @@
 context line
-removed line
+added line
*** End Patch

function.name: process
function.description: Manage background processes started with terminal(background=true). Actions: 'list' (show all), 'poll' (check status + new output), 'log' (full output with pagination), 'wait' (block until done or timeout), 'kill' (terminate), 'write' (send raw stdin data without newline), 'submit' (send data + Enter, for answering prompts), 'close' (close stdin/send EOF).

action.description: Action to perform on background processes

session_id.description: Process session ID (from terminal background output). Required for all actions except 'list'.

data.description: Text to send to process stdin (for 'write' and 'submit' actions)

timeout.description: Max seconds to block for 'wait' action. Returns partial output on timeout.

offset.description: Line offset for 'log' action (default: last 200 lines)

limit.description: Max lines to return for 'log' action

function.name: read_file
function.description: Read a text file with line numbers and pagination. Use this instead of cat/head/tail in terminal. Output format: 'LINE_NUM|CONTENT'. Suggests similar filenames if not found. Use offset and limit for large files. Reads exceeding ~100K characters are rejected; use offset and limit to read specific sections of large files. NOTE: Cannot read images or binary files — use vision_analyze for images.

path.description: Path to the file to read (absolute, relative, or ~/path)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed, default: 1)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read (default: 500, max: 2000)

function.name: search_files
function.description:
Search file contents or find files by name. Use this instead of grep/rg/find/ls in terminal. Ripgrep-backed, faster than shell equivalents.

Content search (target='content'): Regex search inside files. Output modes: full matches with line numbers, file paths only, or match counts.

File search (target='files'): Find files by glob pattern (e.g., '*.py', '*config*'). Also use this instead of ls — results sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: Regex pattern for content search, or glob pattern (e.g., '*.py') for file search

target.description: 'content' searches inside file contents, 'files' searches for files by name

path.description: Directory or file to search in (default: current working directory)

file_glob.description: Filter files by pattern in grep mode (e.g., '*.py' to only search Python files)

limit.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 50)

offset.description: Skip first N results for pagination (default: 0)

output_mode.description: Output format for grep mode: 'content' shows matching lines with line numbers, 'files_only' lists file paths, 'count' shows match counts per file

context.description: Number of context lines before and after each match (grep mode only)

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on a Linux environment. Filesystem usually persists between calls.

Do NOT use cat/head/tail to read files — use read_file instead.
Do NOT use grep/rg/find to search — use search_files instead.
Do NOT use ls to list directories — use search_files(target='files') instead.
Do NOT use sed/awk to edit files — use patch instead.
Do NOT use echo/cat heredoc to create files — use write_file instead.
Reserve terminal for: builds, installs, git, processes, scripts, network, package managers, and anything that needs a shell.

Foreground (default): Commands return INSTANTLY when done, even if the timeout is high. Set timeout=300 for long builds/scripts — you'll still get the result in seconds if it's fast. Prefer foreground for short commands.
Background: Set background=true to get a session_id. Two patterns:
  (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers).
  (2) Long-running tasks with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working on other things and the system auto-notifies you when the task finishes. Great for test suites, builds, deployments, or anything that takes more than a minute.
For servers/watchers, do NOT use shell-level background wrappers (nohup/disown/setsid/trailing '&') in foreground mode. Use background=true so Hermes can track lifecycle and output.
After starting a server, verify readiness with a health check or log signal, then run tests in a separate terminal() call. Avoid blind sleep loops.
Use process(action="poll") for progress checks, process(action="wait") to block until done.
Working directory: Use 'workdir' for per-command cwd.
PTY mode: Set pty=true for interactive CLI tools (Codex, Claude Code, Python REPL).

Do NOT use vim/nano/interactive tools without pty=true — they hang without a pseudo-terminal. Pipe git output to cat if it might page.

command.description: The command to execute on the VM

background.description: Run the command in the background. Two patterns: (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers). (2) Long-running tasks paired with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working and get notified when the task finishes. For short commands, prefer foreground with a generous timeout instead.

timeout.description: Max seconds to wait (default: 180, foreground max: 600). Returns INSTANTLY when command finishes — set high for long tasks, you won't wait unnecessarily. Foreground timeout above 600s is rejected; use background=true for longer commands.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command (absolute path). Defaults to the session working directory.

pty.description: Run in pseudo-terminal (PTY) mode for interactive CLI tools like Codex, Claude Code, or Python REPL. Only works with local and SSH backends. Default: false.

notify_on_complete.description: When true (and background=true), you'll be automatically notified exactly once when the process finishes. **This is the right choice for almost every long-running task** — tests, builds, deployments, multi-item batch jobs, anything that takes over a minute and has a defined end. Use this and keep working on other things; the system notifies you on exit. MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with watch_patterns — when both are set, watch_patterns is dropped.

watch_patterns.description: Strings to watch for in background process output. HARD RATE LIMIT: at most 1 notification per 15 seconds per process — matches arriving inside the cooldown are dropped. After 3 consecutive 15-second windows with dropped matches, watch_patterns is automatically disabled for that process and promoted to notify_on_complete behavior (one notification on exit, no more mid-process spam). USE ONLY for truly rare, one-shot mid-process signals on LONG-LIVED processes that will never exit on their own — e.g. ['Application startup complete'] on a server so you know when to hit its endpoint, or ['migration done'] on a daemon. DO NOT use for: (1) end-of-run markers like 'DONE'/'PASS' — use notify_on_complete instead; (2) error patterns like 'ERROR'/'Traceback' in loops or multi-item batch jobs — they fire on every iteration and you'll hit the strike limit fast; (3) anything you'd ever combine with notify_on_complete. When in doubt, choose notify_on_complete. MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE with notify_on_complete — set one, not both.

Chapter 1 — The Landing Gone Wrong

331| 332|

The descent module Artemis-VII punched through the lunar sky at three thousand meters per second, its heat shield glowing cherry-red against the black. Inside, Dr. Elena Marchetti gripped her harness as the vibration rattled her teeth and the G-forces pressed her deeper into the acceleration couch. Beside her, Commander Jim Hawkes worked the manual override panel with the calm precision of a man who had trained for this exact moment ten thousand times in simulation.

333| 334|

"Twenty kilometers," Hawkes said, his voice flat through the intercom. "Deceleration nominal. Altitude markers matching."

335| 336|

Elena tried to swallow, but her throat was sandpaper. Six months of training in the Arizona desert, three weeks in orbit, and now this final plunge. She was a geologist, not a pilot. Her job was rocks, not rocketry. But the mission had been clear from the start: a six-person geological survey team, forty-five days on the lunar surface, core sampling from the South Pole-Aitken Basin. The most ambitious civilian science expedition ever mounted.

337| 338|

"Ten kilometers," Hawkes continued. "I'm seeing some fluctuation in the braking thrusters. Probably just telemetry lag."

339| 340|

Elena turned her head — a slow, heavy motion under the deceleration — and saw the indicator lights on the auxiliary panel. Two of them were blinking amber. That wasn't in the simulation manual.

341| 342|

"Jim," she said, "check your thruster balance on panel four."

343| 344|

A pause. Eight seconds of silence that felt like hours.

345| 346|

"I see it." Hawkes's voice had lost its flatness. Now it carried an edge Elena had never heard from him before. "We've got asymmetric burn. Starboard thrusters are underperforming by twelve percent."

347| 348|

Twelve percent. Elena's mind raced through the contingency training. Asymmetric burn meant the descent trajectory would drift. The automated guidance would try to compensate, but the margins on a lunar landing were razor-thin. There was no atmosphere to slow them, no parachutes, no backup systems beyond what was bolted to the hull.

349| 350|

"Can we correct?" she asked.

351| 352|

"Already trying. Switching to manual guidance mode." Hawkes's hands moved across the console, entering override codes. "Elena, I need you to call out altitude and vertical velocity from the secondary display. My panel's prioritizing attitude control."

353| 354|

Elena unclenched her fingers from the armrest and forced them toward the secondary screen. The numbers swam for a moment before resolving: altitude 4,200 meters, vertical velocity 62 meters per second, horizontal drift 180 meters and increasing.

355| 356|

"Four thousand meters, velocity sixty-two, drift one-eighty and climbing."

357| 358|

"Copy. Engaging correction burn."

359| 360|

The module shuddered as the port-side thrusters fired harder, trying to compensate for their lazy starboard counterparts. Elena felt the shift in vector, a sideways push that pressed her against the left side of her harness. The drift reading flickered: 175 meters. 170. 162.

361| 362|

"It's working," she breathed.

363| 364|

"Don't celebrate yet. Three thousand meters."

365| 366|

The ground was visible now through the forward viewport — not the smooth, gray plain she had expected, but a jumble of crater rims and ridges, sharp shadows cutting across the surface at oblique angles. They were coming in hot, and the terrain below was anything but flat.

367| 368|

"Two thousand meters. Drift stabilizing at forty meters. Thrusters at eighty-five percent."

369| 370|

A warning chime cut through the cabin. Elena's eyes snapped to the diagnostic panel. "Jim, the starboard thruster temperature is spiking. It's overheating."

371| 372|

"I see it. Shutting it down before it blows."

373| 374|

"If you shut it down, we lose half our braking—"

375| 376|

"I know."

377| 378|

The starboard thruster cut out with a clunk that Elena felt through the deck plates. The module immediately began to yaw, the horizon spinning past the viewport in a nauseating blur. Hawkes fought the controls, compensating with the remaining thrusters, but the descent had become a controlled fall rather than a landing.

379| 380|

"Five hundred meters. Velocity still forty-five. We're going to hit hard."

381| 382|

Elena braced herself, pressing her spine into the couch. The ground rushed up — a gray wall of rock and shadow — and then the remaining thrusters fired in a last desperate burn, kicking up a cloud of regolith that blotted out everything.

383| 384|

The impact was not a crash. It was worse: a grinding, tearing, skidding collision that threw Elena forward against her harness and filled the cabin with the screech of metal on stone. The module tipped, slid, and came to rest at an angle that left her hanging sideways, her vision swimming with stars and dust.

385| 386|

Silence. Then the hiss of escaping atmosphere.

387| 388|

"Jim?" Elena's voice was a rasp. "Jim, are you there?"

389| 390|

A groan from the command seat. "I'm here. I think my arm is broken. And we've got a hull breach."

391| 392|

Elena forced her eyes open and saw the red warning lights painting the cabin like a crime scene. They were down. They were alive. But the module was crippled, and somewhere in the chain of systems that had been designed to keep them alive for forty-five days, a dozen things were now broken.

393| 394|

The mission had become something else entirely.

395| 396|

It had become a fight for survival.

397|

* * *

398|

* * *

399|

Elena checked her oxygen gauge, watching the numbers tick down with grim certainty. Fifteen percent. The module's cold was seeping through her suit, her fingers numb, her breath fogging the inside of her visor. They had lost so much already — crew members, equipment, hope. But she refused to let them lose everything.

400|

"We can do this," she said, more to herself than to the others. "We have to do this."

401|

Hawkes nodded, his face set with determination. "Then let's stop talking and start moving."

402|

* * *

403|

* * *

404|

"The ice is processing," Yuki reported, watching the electrolysis unit's display. "We've got another twelve hours of oxygen. Maybe fourteen if we keep activity to minimum." She looked exhausted, dark circles under her eyes, but there was hope in her voice for the first time in days.

405|

"That's enough for one more expedition into the network," Elena said. "One more chance to find the control center."

406|

"And if we don't find it?" Mensah asked.

407|

"Then we try something else." Elena met her eyes. "We're not done yet. None of us are."

408|

* * *

409|

* * *

410|

"I've been analyzing the crystal's resonance frequency," Yuki said, her voice tight with excitement. "It's not random. It's a carrier wave. There's data modulated onto it — information, encoded in the same way our radio waves carry sound." She pulled up the waveform on her tablet. "If we can decode this, we might be able to communicate with the network directly."

411|

"Communicate how?" Hawkes asked.

412|

"The same way the sphere communicated with Elena. Through direct neural interface. The crystal is broadcasting on a frequency that bypasses language entirely." Yuki looked up, her eyes bright. "The builders didn't just leave us a library. They left us a teacher."

413| 414|
415| 416|

Chapter 02

417| 418|

Chapter 2 — Emergency Protocols

Elena's training took over before her conscious mind caught up. Her hands moved through the emergency shutdown sequence: main power off, auxiliary batteries online, cabin pressure isolation valves closed. The hissing stopped. The cabin grew quiet, save for the tick of cooling metal and the ragged sound of her own breathing.

421|

* * *

422|

"Listen to me," Elena said, her voice cracking through the helmet speaker. She held up the oxygen gauge so everyone could see. "We have forty-three hours of breathable air. Forty-three. That's not enough time for a rescue mission from Earth. That's not enough time for anything except sitting here and watching each other suffocate." She looked at Hawkes, whose broken arm hung in a sling. "Unless we do something."

423|

"Do what?" Mensah asked. "We're in a broken module on a dead world. We don't have thrusters, we don't have a working comms array, and half our supplies are in a compartment that's open to vacuum."

424|

"We have ice," Yuki said quietly. Everyone turned to look at her. "The geological survey data showed water ice in the permanently shadowed craters. If Elena can reach it, if she can bring back enough to run through the electrolysis system, we can extend our oxygen by days."

425|

Hawkes shook his head. "That's three kilometers across unexplored terrain. In an EVA suit. With no support vehicle."

426|

"It's three kilometers to survival," Elena said. "I'm going."

427|

* * *

428|

Elena's fingers were numb inside her gloves. She'd been working for twenty minutes straight, trying to patch the hull breach with the emergency kit, and the epoxy wasn't setting properly in the vacuum. Each time she applied a layer, it bubbled and peeled, refusing to bond with the cold metal. Behind her, through the cracked viewport, she could see the Earth hanging in the black sky — blue and white and impossibly distant.

429|

"How's it going out there?" Hawkes's voice crackled through the comms.

430|

"Terribly. The epoxy won't cure." Elena pressed another strip of patch material against the torn hull, holding it in place with her palm. "I need heat to make it bond. Can you route auxiliary power to the exterior repair ports?"

431|

A pause. "That'll drain our batteries faster."

432|

"And if I don't seal this breach, we'll lose atmosphere faster. Pick your poison."

433|

She felt the module vibrate as Hawkes rerouted power. The patch material began to warm beneath her hand, the epoxy finally setting. She held it there, counting seconds, not daring to move until she was sure it would hold.

434|

* * *

435|

"I'm telling you, the walls are warm," Elena said, pressing her gloved hand against the tunnel surface. "Not ambient warmth from the Moon's core. Something active. Something generating heat." She looked back at Okafor, whose lamp beam cut a narrow cone through the darkness. "Feel it."

436|

Okafor touched the wall and his eyes widened. "That's... that's not natural. The thermal conductivity of lunar basalt wouldn't produce this kind of uniform temperature."

437|

"Exactly." Elena moved deeper into the passage, her lamp revealing symbols on the walls — spirals and patterns that seemed to shift when she looked directly at them. "This tunnel was made. Or grown. I don't know which."

438|

"Grown?"

439|

"Like a tree branch. Or a blood vessel." She turned to face him, her face invisible behind the reflective visor. "I think we just found something that changes everything."

440|

* * *

441|

A warning chime cut through the silence. Elena glanced at her wrist display and felt her blood turn to ice. "My suit temperature is dropping. The heating element in the left boot failed." She stamped her foot, trying to restore circulation. "I can't feel my toes anymore."

442|

"You need to get back to the module," Hawkes said over the comms. "Frostbite in a vacuum is no joke. The tissue damage is irreversible."

443|

"I'm half a kilometer from the crater rim. If I turn back now, I lose three hours of daylight." She kept walking, her gait becoming uneven as the numbness spread up her ankle. "I can make it."

444|

"Elena —"

445|

"I can make it, Jim. Trust me." She gritted her teeth and pushed forward, each step sending a lance of cold up her leg. The crater rim was visible now, a dark ridge against the starfield. Behind it lay the ice. Behind it lay their survival. She limped on, refusing to stop.

446| 447|

"Status report," she said, the words coming out as a command despite the tremor in her voice. "Jim, give me a full systems assessment."

448| 449|

Hawkes was already running diagnostics with his good arm, his face pale under the emergency lighting. "Primary power: offline. We lost the main bus in the impact. Auxiliary power at forty percent and dropping — we're running on batteries until the solar panels deploy, and I don't know if the deployment mechanism survived."

450| 451|

Elena unclipped her harness and floated — or rather, fell — sideways out of her seat. The one-sixth gravity made the motion disorienting, her limbs moving faster than she expected. She caught herself on a bulkhead and pushed toward the equipment locker.

452| 453|

"Hull integrity?" she asked, pulling out the emergency medical kit.

454| 455|

"Three breaches that I can see. Small ones — micrometeorite shielding took most of the damage. But we've lost pressure in the aft compartment. It's isolated now, but that's where half our food supplies are stored."

456|

* * *

457|

"Look at this," Yuki said, pulling up a spectral analysis on her tablet. The graph showed a spike at a wavelength none of them had seen before. "The ice samples aren't just water. There's something mixed in at the molecular level. Organic compounds." She zoomed in on the reading. "Amino acids. Not the standard ones — these have a different chirality than anything found on Earth."

458|

"That's impossible," Mensah said, leaning in. "Amino acids in lunar ice? From what source?"

459|

"Cometary impacts can deposit organic material, but this concentration is too high. And the structure..." Yuki paused, frowning at the screen. "The structure suggests synthesis. Deliberate, controlled synthesis."

460|

Elena felt a chill run down her spine. "You're saying someone produced these amino acids. In the ice. Beneath the Moon."

461|

"I'm saying the builders might not have just lived here. They might have been preparing the environment for something. Or someone."

462| 463|

Elena landed beside Hawkes and opened the med kit. His arm was bent at an angle that made her stomach lurch, the forearm swelling visibly even through the pressure suit he still wore. "This is going to hurt," she said.

464| 465|

"It already hurts. Just set it and wrap it. We don't have time for delicacy."

466| 467|

She worked quickly, splinting the fracture with the rigid supports from the kit and binding it tight with elastic bandages. Hawkes's breathing was controlled but shallow, his teeth clenched. When she finished, he was sweating despite the cabin's cool temperature.

468| 469|

"The rest of the crew," Elena said. "We need to check on them. The rear module—"

470| 471|

"Is depressurized," Hawkes finished. "But they had emergency suits. If they got them on in time—"

472|

* * *

473|

Elena sat alone at the edge of the crevasse, her legs dangling over the drop into darkness. The stars above were brilliant, unwinking, and the Earth glowed like a blue gem against the black. She had been sitting here for ten minutes, just breathing, letting the vastness of space remind her how small her problems were in the grand scale of things.

474|

"Mind if I join you?" Hawkes's voice came from behind her. He eased himself down beside her, his broken arm cradled in its sling. "I used to do this on my first deployment. Sit and stare. It helps."

475|

"Does it ever stop feeling so... big?" she asked.

476|

"No. But you learn to appreciate it instead of being afraid of it." He looked up at the Earth. "See that? That's home. And we're going back there. All of us."

477|

"You sound certain."

478|

"I have to be. If I'm not certain, then what's the point of any of this?"

479|

Elena nodded slowly. She looked down into the crevasse, where the blue glow of the builder platform pulsed faintly. "What do you think they wanted? The builders. Why build all this and then leave?"

480|

"Maybe they didn't leave. Maybe they just... changed." Hawkes shrugged. "Or maybe they're still here, and we just can't see them."

481| 482|

A thump from the aft hatch cut him off. Three short knocks. The emergency signal. Elena scrambled across the angled deck and pressed her helmet against the hatch, activating the external microphone.

483| 484|

"Identify yourself."

485| 486|

"It's Tanaka." The voice was muffled but unmistakable — Dr. Yuki Tanaka, the mission's astrobiologist. "I've got Dr. Kowalski with me. He's unconscious. We need medical assistance."

487| 488|

Elena checked the pressure gauge beside the hatch. The aft compartment was reading zero, but the emergency airlock between the sections still held pressure. She cycled the lock, watching the numbers drop and rise, and when the inner door opened, Yuki half-carried, half-floated the limp form of Dr. Martin Kowalski into the forward cabin.

489| 490|

Kowalski's face was pale, his lips tinged blue. His suit showed a tear across the upper arm where a piece of debris had caught him during the decompression. Yuki had applied a temporary patch, but the exposure to vacuum had already done its damage.

491|

* * *

492|

"The oxygen level is critical," Yuki announced, her voice flat. "We have maybe six hours before the partial pressure drops below survivable thresholds. The scrubbers are failing faster than I predicted." She turned from the display, her face gray in the emergency lighting. "I'm sorry. I've done everything I can."

493|

"You have nothing to apologize for," Elena said. She stood up, her joints aching from days of crouching in the cramped module. "Six hours. That's enough time for one more attempt."

494|

"Elena, no. You can't go back out there. Your suit is damaged, your oxygen consumption is elevated —"

495|

"I can make it to the ice deposit and back in four hours. That gives us two hours of margin." She was already reaching for her helmet. "I'm not going to sit here and wait to die, Yuki. I'm going to fight."

496|

Yuki watched her for a long moment, then nodded. "Then I'll make sure the electrolysis system is ready when you get back."

497|

"When," Elena repeated. "Not if."

498| 499|

"How long was he exposed?" Hawkes asked, already reaching for the oxygen mask.

"I can make it to the ice deposit and back in four hours. That gives us two hours of margin." She was already reaching for her helmet. "I'm not going to sit here and wait to die, Yuki. I'm going to fight."

1001|

Yuki watched her for a long moment, then nodded. "Then I'll make sure the electrolysis system is ready when you get back."

1002|

"When," Elena repeated. "Not if."

1003| 1004|

"What do you mean?"

1005| 1006|

Elena moved toward the tunnel, her lamp casting long shadows ahead of her. The walls were smooth, too smooth to be natural. They had the look of something shaped by heat and flow — a lava tube, perhaps, but one that had been modified. Widened. Smoothed.

1007| 1008|

"I mean," she said, "that someone — or something — has been here before us."

1009|

* * *

1010|

* * *

1011|

Hawkes stared at the navigation display, his good hand gripping the edge of the console. The numbers told a grim story: their position had shifted during the crash landing, and the emergency beacons they had deployed were transmitting from a location nearly two kilometers from their actual position. If a rescue mission came looking for them, they would search the wrong coordinates.

1012|

"We need to move the beacons," he said. "Or we need to reach the actual landing site and activate the secondary transponder there."

1013|

"That's a ten-kilometer walk," Okafor said. "In EVA suits. Across terrain we've never surveyed."

1014|

"I know." Hawkes met his eyes. "But if we don't, no one will ever find us."

1015|

Okafor was silent for a moment. Then he said, "I'll go with you."

1016|

"No. You're needed here. I'll go alone."

1017|

"With a broken arm?"

1018|

"I'll manage." Hawkes smiled grimly. "I've done more with less."

1019|

* * *

1020|

"The ice is processing," Yuki reported, watching the electrolysis unit's display. "We've got another twelve hours of oxygen. Maybe fourteen if we keep activity to minimum." She looked exhausted, dark circles under her eyes, but there was hope in her voice for the first time in days.

1021|

"That's enough for one more expedition into the network," Elena said. "One more chance to find the control center."

1022|

"And if we don't find it?" Mensah asked.

1023|

"Then we try something else." Elena met her eyes. "We're not done yet. None of us are."

1024|

* * *

1025|

* * *

1026|

"I'm not saying we abandon the module," Mensah said, her voice rising. "I'm saying we need a contingency plan. If the solar storm intensifies, if the radiation levels become lethal, we can't stay here. We need somewhere to go."

1027|

"And you propose moving into an alien structure that we've mapped for less than twenty-four hours?" Hawkes shook his head. "That's not a contingency. That's suicide."

1028|

"It's a risk assessment. The network chambers are deeper, more shielded, and they're generating their own heat. The temperature down there is survivable without suit heaters. Up here, we're freezing to death."

1029|

"We don't know what's down there."

1030|

"We don't know what's up here either," Elena cut in. "We know the module is dying. We know the oxygen is running out. And we know there's something under the crater that might save us." She looked at Hawkes. "I trust the science. And the science says the network is our best option."

1031|

Hawkes held her gaze for a long moment, then looked away. "Fine. But we do this methodically. No rushing. No heroics."

1032|

* * *

1033|

"I've been analyzing the crystal's resonance frequency," Yuki said, her voice tight with excitement. "It's not random. It's a carrier wave. There's data modulated onto it — information, encoded in the same way our radio waves carry sound." She pulled up the waveform on her tablet. "If we can decode this, we might be able to communicate with the network directly."

1034|

"Communicate how?" Hawkes asked.

1035|

"The same way the sphere communicated with Elena. Through direct neural interface. The crystal is broadcasting on a frequency that bypasses language entirely." Yuki looked up, her eyes bright. "The builders didn't just leave us a library. They left us a teacher."

1036| 1037|
1038| 1039|

Chapter 06

1040| 1041|

Chapter 6 — Water Ice Gamble

The tunnel stretched ahead of Elena, its walls gleaming with a patina of ice that reflected her lamp beam in fractured rainbows. She moved cautiously, testing each step before committing her weight, her injured ribs protesting with every breath. The passage was wide enough for two people to walk abreast, the ceiling high enough that she could stand upright without stooping. It was not a natural formation.

1044| 1045|

"I'm exploring a tunnel system beneath the ice layer," she reported. The radio signal was weak, barely maintaining contact, but she could hear Yuki's responses through a hail of static. "The walls show signs of thermal modification. This might be an ancient lava tube, but the dimensions are uniform — too uniform for a random geological feature."

1046|

* * *

1047|

"I'm telling you, the walls are warm," Elena said, pressing her gloved hand against the tunnel surface. "Not ambient warmth from the Moon's core. Something active. Something generating heat." She looked back at Okafor, whose lamp beam cut a narrow cone through the darkness. "Feel it."

1048|

Okafor touched the wall and his eyes widened. "That's... that's not natural. The thermal conductivity of lunar basalt wouldn't produce this kind of uniform temperature."

1049|

"Exactly." Elena moved deeper into the passage, her lamp revealing symbols on the walls — spirals and patterns that seemed to shift when she looked directly at them. "This tunnel was made. Or grown. I don't know which."

1050|

"Grown?"

1051|

"Like a tree branch. Or a blood vessel." She turned to face him, her face invisible behind the reflective visor. "I think we just found something that changes everything."

1052| 1053|

"Could it be a fracture zone from an impact?" Yuki's voice asked, breaking up. "Some impacts create — systematic fault patterns —"

1054| 1055|

"No. This is different. The walls have been smoothed. There are tool marks — or at least, marks that look like tool marks."

1056| 1057|

She ran her gloved hand along the wall. The surface was cold, even through the insulation of her suit, and it had a texture she could not quite identify. Not rough like fractured basalt, not smooth like polished stone. Something in between, as if the material had been melted and then rapidly cooled.

1058| 1059|

The tunnel curved to the left, then straightened, then opened into a chamber that made Elena stop in her tracks.

1060| 1061|

The chamber was enormous — perhaps fifty meters across, with a ceiling that disappeared into darkness above the range of her lamp. The floor was flat, impossibly flat, as if it had been leveled by machinery. And arranged across that floor, in concentric rings that radiated from a central point, were structures.

1062|

* * *

1063|

"Look at this," Yuki said, pulling up a spectral analysis on her tablet. The graph showed a spike at a wavelength none of them had seen before. "The ice samples aren't just water. There's something mixed in at the molecular level. Organic compounds." She zoomed in on the reading. "Amino acids. Not the standard ones — these have a different chirality than anything found on Earth."

1064|

"That's impossible," Mensah said, leaning in. "Amino acids in lunar ice? From what source?"

1065|

"Cometary impacts can deposit organic material, but this concentration is too high. And the structure..." Yuki paused, frowning at the screen. "The structure suggests synthesis. Deliberate, controlled synthesis."

1066|

Elena felt a chill run down her spine. "You're saying someone produced these amino acids. In the ice. Beneath the Moon."

1067|

"I'm saying the builders might not have just lived here. They might have been preparing the environment for something. Or someone."

1068| 1069|

They were not buildings in any human sense. They were low, domed shapes, their surfaces dark and vitreous, like obsidian that had been poured into molds and allowed to cool. Each dome was about three meters in diameter, with a single opening at the base that faced the center of the chamber. There were dozens of them, arranged with geometric precision that could not be natural.

1070| 1071|

Elena's scientific mind struggled to categorize what she was seeing. Natural formations? No — the symmetry was too perfect. Human structures? Impossible — no human mission had ever reached this location. The answer that remained was one she could barely bring herself to consider.

1072| 1073|

"Yuki," she said, her voice barely above a whisper, "I need you to record everything I'm about to describe. I'm sending you a data burst with the coordinates. If I don't make it back, this data has to reach Earth."

1074| 1075|

"Elena, what are you seeing?"

1076| 1077|

She described the chamber, the domes, the impossible geometry. She described the way the structures seemed to absorb light rather than reflect it, the way the airless silence of the cavern seemed to press against her suit as if the space itself was listening. She described the symbols — if they were symbols — carved into the central platform, a spiral pattern that coiled inward toward a dark core.

1078|

* * *

1079|

The crystal chamber was quiet now. The sphere had stopped glowing, the symbols had dimmed, and the only light came from Elena's helmet lamp. She stood alone in the center of the room, her hand still pressed against the pedestal where the sphere had rested.

1080|

The vision had faded, but its echoes remained. She had seen the builders — not as forms, but as patterns of light and energy, weaving through the lunar rock like thoughts through a mind. They had been beautiful. They had been terrifying. And they had been alone, for so long, waiting for someone to find them.

1081|

"What did they show you?" Mensah asked from the entrance.

1082|

Elena turned. "They showed me that intelligence doesn't have to be biological. That consciousness can exist in forms we can't imagine. That the universe is stranger and more wonderful than we ever dreamed." She paused. "And they showed me that we're not the first. And we won't be the last."

1083| 1084|

"I'm going to approach one of the domes," she said. "I need samples. I need evidence."

1085| 1086|

"Elena, wait —"

1087| 1088|

But she was already moving, crossing the level floor toward the nearest dome. The material under her boots was not regolith but something else — a compacted surface that felt almost like ceramic. Her footsteps made no sound in the vacuum, and the silence was absolute, broken only by the hum of her suit's systems and the pounding of her own heart.

1089| 1090|

The dome's opening was a perfect arch, its edges smooth and regular. She shone her lamp inside and saw a space that was small and empty, its floor marked with the same spiral pattern as the central platform. Whatever had lived here — if anything had lived here — was long gone.

1091| 1092|

She reached out and touched the interior wall. The material was warm.

1093|

* * *

1094|

"The oxygen level is critical," Yuki announced, her voice flat. "We have maybe six hours before the partial pressure drops below survivable thresholds. The scrubbers are failing faster than I predicted." She turned from the display, her face gray in the emergency lighting. "I'm sorry. I've done everything I can."

1095|

"You have nothing to apologize for," Elena said. She stood up, her joints aching from days of crouching in the cramped module. "Six hours. That's enough time for one more attempt."

1096|

"Elena, no. You can't go back out there. Your suit is damaged, your oxygen consumption is elevated —"

1097|

"I can make it to the ice deposit and back in four hours. That gives us two hours of margin." She was already reaching for her helmet. "I'm not going to sit here and wait to die, Yuki. I'm going to fight."

1098|

Yuki watched her for a long moment, then nodded. "Then I'll make sure the electrolysis system is ready when you get back."

1099|

"When," Elena repeated. "Not if."

1100| 1101|

Not warm from proximity to the surface. Warm as if something inside the dome was generating heat. She pressed her palm flat against the surface and felt a faint vibration, a pulse so subtle she might have imagined it.

1102| 1103|

"There's residual heat," she reported. "These structures are not dead. They're — I don't know the word for it. Dormant, maybe. Waiting."

1104| 1105|

"Waiting for what?" Yuki asked.

1106| 1107|

Elena did not answer. She was looking at the spiral pattern on the floor, and she had realized something that made the hair on the back of her neck stand up. The spiral had exactly seven turns. It was not a random design. It was a countdown.

1108|

* * *

1109|

* * *

1110|

"The seventh tunnel is the key," Okafor insisted, tapping his finger on the schematic he had drawn. "Look at the pattern. Six chambers arranged in a hexagon around the central platform. Six tunnels radiating outward. But there's a seventh — hidden, locked, waiting for something."

1111|

"You're making assumptions based on incomplete data," Mensah said.

1112|

"I'm making observations. The builders thought in sevens. The spiral has seven turns. The signal has seven pulses. There are seven tunnels — we just haven't found the entrance to the last one yet."

1113|

Elena studied the schematic. Okafor was right about the pattern. Seven was the constant, the thread that ran through everything. "Where's the entrance?" she asked.

1114|

"I think it's in the main chamber. Hidden in the spiral itself." Okafor pointed at the center of the diagram. "The spiral arms aren't random. Each arm points to one of the visible tunnels. But the seventh arm — the one that should complete the pattern — points to a blank section of wall."

1115|

"Then that's where we look," Elena said.

1116|

* * *

1117|

Elena checked her oxygen gauge, watching the numbers tick down with grim certainty. Fifteen percent. The module's cold was seeping through her suit, her fingers numb, her breath fogging the inside of her visor. They had lost so much already — crew members, equipment, hope. But she refused to let them lose everything.

1118|

"We can do this," she said, more to herself than to the others. "We have to do this."

1119|

Hawkes nodded, his face set with determination. "Then let's stop talking and start moving."

1120| 1121|

She backed out of the dome, her pulse racing. Whatever this place was, whatever intelligence had built it, it was not a relic of the distant past. It was something current, something active, and she had just walked into the middle of it with nothing more than a geological sampling kit and a rapidly depleting oxygen tank.

1122| 1123|

She needed ice. She needed oxygen. She needed to get back to the module and figure out what to do with the discovery she had just made.

1124|

* * *

1125|

A warning chime cut through the silence. Elena glanced at her wrist display and felt her blood turn to ice. "My suit temperature is dropping. The heating element in the left boot failed." She stamped her foot, trying to restore circulation. "I can't feel my toes anymore."

1126|

"You need to get back to the module," Hawkes said over the comms. "Frostbite in a vacuum is no joke. The tissue damage is irreversible."

1127|

"I'm half a kilometer from the crater rim. If I turn back now, I lose three hours of daylight." She kept walking, her gait becoming uneven as the numbness spread up her ankle. "I can make it."

1128|

"Elena —"

1129|

"I can make it, Jim. Trust me." She gritted her teeth and pushed forward, each step sending a lance of cold up her leg. The crater rim was visible now, a dark ridge against the starfield. Behind it lay the ice. Behind it lay their survival. She limped on, refusing to stop.

1130| 1131|

But as she turned to retrace her steps, she noticed something that stopped her cold. The tunnel she had come through was no longer the only exit from the chamber. On the far side, visible now in the full sweep of her lamp, there were three more openings, equally spaced around the circumference of the room. They had not been there when she entered.

1132| 1133|

The chamber had changed while she was inside the dome.

1134| 1135|

"Yuki," she said, her voice tight, "I think I need to get out of here. Now."

1136|

* * *

1137|

Sarah's hands were raw from gripping the same valve for three hours. She couldn't feel her fingers anymore. But every time she thought about stopping, she pictured David's face — the way he'd looked at her before the extraction team left, trusting her to bring help. She hadn't brought help. She'd brought herself, and that would have to be enough. They knew that the window of opportunity was narrow — that every moment of delay could mean the difference between success and failure. The stakes were simply too high to allow for hesitation or doubt.

1138|

* * *

1139|

Elena stared at the radiation readings, running the numbers three times to make sure she wasn't making a mistake. "The chamber walls are emitting energy. Not much — a few milliwatts per square meter — but it's consistent. Uniform across every surface." She looked up at the others. "This isn't residual heat from volcanic activity. The walls are generating power."

1140|

"How?" Hawkes asked.

1141|

"I don't know. Some kind of piezoelectric effect, maybe. Or something we don't have a name for." She pressed her hand against the obsidian surface. It was warm, as always, vibrating with that same subtle frequency. "The entire network might be one giant power generator. If we can tap into it —"

1142|

"We could run our equipment indefinitely," Mensah finished. "We could heat the module. We could recharge our suits. We could —"

1143|

"We could survive," Elena said. "As long as we need to."

1144|

"We have seventy-two hours," Sarah said. "Maybe less. The water reclamation system is failing faster than the models predicted." She looked around the table at the drawn faces of her team. "I'm not going to lie to you. The odds are bad. But I've been in bad odds before. We all have. And we're still here." "Slowly. But it's happening."

1145|

The news was met with a mixture of relief and renewed determination. They had been working toward this moment for so long that the prospect of success seemed almost unreal. But here it was — tangible, measurable, within reach.

1146|

"Keep going," came the reply. "We're almost there."

1147|

* * *

1148|

Elena reviewed the data from the electrolysis system, calculating their remaining oxygen with precision. The numbers were stark but not hopeless — if they could find another ice deposit, they could stretch their supply another three days. But every hour they spent searching was an hour closer to suffocation.

1149|

* * *

1150|

Elena sat alone at the edge of the crevasse, her legs dangling over the drop into darkness. The stars above were brilliant, unwinking, and the Earth glowed like a blue gem against the black. She had been sitting here for ten minutes, just breathing, letting the vastness of space remind her how small her problems were in the grand scale of things.

1151|

"Mind if I join you?" Hawkes's voice came from behind her. He eased himself down beside her, his broken arm cradled in its sling. "I used to do this on my first deployment. Sit and stare. It helps."

1152|

"Does it ever stop feeling so... big?" she asked.

1153|

"No. But you learn to appreciate it instead of being afraid of it." He looked up at the Earth. "See that? That's home. And we're going back there. All of us."

1154|

"You sound certain."

1155|

"I have to be. If I'm not certain, then what's the point of any of this?"

1156|

Elena nodded slowly. She looked down into the crevasse, where the blue glow of the builder platform pulsed faintly. "What do you think they wanted? The builders. Why build all this and then leave?"

1157|

"Maybe they didn't leave. Maybe they just... changed." Hawkes shrugged. "Or maybe they're still here, and we just can't see them."

1158|

"Run it again," Sarah ordered. The technician's fingers hesitated over the keyboard. "We've run it three times. The results are the same." "Then run it a fourth time. Because if those numbers are right, everything we know about our water supply is wrong." The technician ran it again. The numbers came back the same. And Sarah felt the ground shift beneath her feet. "Unless —" They paused, a new thought forming. "Unless we've been looking at it wrong the whole time."

1159|

The idea was met with skepticism at first. But as they worked through the implications, a new understanding began to emerge. They had been asking the wrong questions. Now they knew what to ask. And the answers were waiting.

1160| 1161|
1162| 1163|

Chapter 07

1164| 1165|

Chapter 7 — Communication Blackout

The return journey was a nightmare of disorientation and fear. Elena found the original tunnel — or thought she did — but the passage seemed different now, its walls marked with symbols she did not remember seeing before. She moved as quickly as her injured ribs and dwindling oxygen allowed, her lamp beam dancing across surfaces that seemed to shift in the periphery of her vision.

1168| 1169|

The crevasse by which she had entered was still there, the broken ice forming a jagged skylight above. She climbed the debris slope, her boots scrabbling for purchase, and hauled herself through the gap onto the crater floor. The sunlight, when she reached it, was blinding after the darkness below.

1170| 1171|

She did not stop to rest. She had been gone for over four hours, and her oxygen was down to the red zone. She ran — or as close to running as the EVA suit allowed — covering the three kilometers back to the module in a desperate, sustained effort that left her gasping and dizzy.

1172|

* * *

1173|

Hawkes stared at the navigation display, his good hand gripping the edge of the console. "We need to move the beacons," he said. "Or we need to reach the actual landing site and activate the secondary transponder there."

1175|

"That's a ten-kilometer walk," Okafor said. "In EVA suits. Across terrain we've never surveyed."

1176|

"I know." Hawkes met his eyes. "But if we don't, no one will ever find us."

1177|

Okafor was silent for a moment. Then he said, "I'll go with you."

1178|

"No. You're needed here. I'll go alone."

1179|

"With a broken arm?"

1180|

"I'll manage." Hawkes smiled grimly. "I've done more with less."

1181|

* * *

1182|

"I'm not saying we abandon the module," Mensah said, her voice rising. "I'm saying we need a contingency plan. If the solar storm intensifies, if the radiation levels become lethal, we can't stay here. We need somewhere to go."

1183|

"And you propose moving into an alien structure that we've mapped for less than twenty-four hours?" Hawkes shook his head. "That's not a contingency. That's suicide."

1184|

"It's a risk assessment. The network chambers are deeper, more shielded, and they're generating their own heat. The temperature down there is survivable without suit heaters. Up here, we're freezing to death."

1185|

"We don't know what's down there."

1186|

"We don't know what's up here either," Elena cut in. "We know the module is dying. We know the oxygen is running out. And we know there's something under the crater that might save us." She looked at Hawkes. "I trust the science. And the science says the network is our best option."

1187|

Hawkes held her gaze for a long moment, then looked away. "Fine. But we do this methodically. No rushing. No heroics."

1188| 1189|

The airlock cycled, and she collapsed inside, tearing off her helmet and gulping the thin, recycled air of the forward cabin. Yuki was there, checking her vitals, asking questions she could not answer coherently.

1190| 1191|

"I found something," Elena said finally, when she had caught her breath. "Under the crater. A chamber. Structures. Domes, arranged in rings. And symbols — spirals — that look like they mean something."

1192| 1193|

The crew gathered around her, their faces a mixture of disbelief and concern. Hawkes, his arm in a sling, listened without interrupting. Okafor and Mensah exchanged glances that spoke of shared skepticism. Only Yuki seemed to take her at her word, her astrobiologist's mind already racing through the implications.

1194| 1195|

"Could it be a natural formation?" Hawkes asked. "Lava tubes can create some unusual geometries."

1196| 1197|

"No," Elena said. "I've studied lava tubes. I've mapped them, sampled them, published papers on them. The structures I saw were not natural. They were designed."

1198|

* * *

1199|

"The seventh tunnel is the key," Okafor insisted, tapping his finger on the schematic he had drawn. "Look at the pattern. Six chambers arranged in a hexagon around the central platform. Six tunnels radiating outward. But there's a seventh — hidden, locked, waiting for something."

1200|

1201|

"I'm making observations. The builders thought in sevens. The spiral has seven turns. The signal has seven pulses. There are seven tunnels — we just haven't found the entrance to the last one yet."

1202|

Elena studied the schematic. Okafor was right about the pattern. Seven was the constant, the thread that ran through everything. "Where's the entrance?" she asked.

1203|

"I think it's in the main chamber. Hidden in the spiral itself." Okafor pointed at the center of the diagram. "The spiral arms aren't random. Each arm points to one of the visible tunnels. But the seventh arm — the one that should complete the pattern — points to a blank section of wall."

1204|

"Then that's where we look," Elena said.

1205| 1206|

"By who? No human mission has ever reached the South Pole-Aitken Basin, and the orbital surveys would have detected any previous human activity."

1207| 1208|

"I know. That's what worries me."

1209| 1210|

Kowalski, still weak from his vacuum exposure, spoke up from his cot. "If Elena is correct, we have a responsibility to document this discovery. Whatever it is, it could be the most significant find in human history."

1211| 1212|

"If we survive long enough to report it," Mensah said. "Our oxygen situation hasn't improved. Elena brought back ice samples, but we still need to process them, and that takes power we don't have."

1213| 1214|

The discussion was interrupted by a burst of static from the comms console. Yuki rushed to it, adjusting the frequency. "I'm picking up something — a signal. Weak, but it's structured. It's not natural."

1215|

* * *

1216|

"We're not going to make it, are we?" Kowalski's voice was barely a whisper. He lay on the cot, his face pale, the vacuum exposure having left him weak and breathless. Yuki adjusted his IV drip, avoiding his eyes. "You can tell me. I'd rather know."

1217|

"We're going to make it," Yuki said, but her voice lacked conviction. She checked his pupils, his pulse, the oxygen saturation in his blood. "We have a plan. Elena is out there getting ice. We're going to stretch the oxygen."

1218|

"And if she doesn't come back?"

1219|

Yuki finally met his gaze. "Then we figure out something else. That's what we do here. We survive." She squeezed his hand. "Now rest. Conserve your strength."

1220|

He closed his eyes, and Yuki turned away, pressing her fist against her mouth. The module was cold, so cold, and the oxygen gauge was dropping faster than her models predicted. She didn't know if they would make it. She was a scientist, not a miracle worker. But she would keep pretending until the very end.

1221| 1222|

"Is it Earth?" Elena asked.

1223| 1224|

"No. The frequency is wrong. It's —" Yuki paused, her hands frozen on the controls. "It's coming from the same direction as the crater you explored."

1225| 1226|

The room went quiet.

1227| 1228|

"It's a repeating pattern," Yuki continued. "A sequence of pulses. Seven pulses, a pause, then seven again. It's been transmitting this whole time, but we didn't have the right equipment to detect it."

1229| 1230|

"The countdown," Elena whispered. "The spiral had seven turns. The pulses repeat in sets of seven."

1231|

* * *

1232|

"The spiral pattern appears in every chamber," Yuki said, tracing the symbol on her tablet. "But the number of rotations varies. Some have three turns, some have five, some have seven. I think it's a numbering system." She pulled up images from four different chambers. "Three means one thing, five means another. Seven appears in the most important locations — the control center, the main platform, the door that wouldn't open."

1233|

"So seven is significant," Elena said. "The most significant number."

1234|

"In many ancient Earth cultures, seven represented completion. The seven classical planets, the seven days of the week, the seven notes of the diatonic scale." Yuki zoomed in on the seven-turn spiral. "The builders might have shared that symbolism. Or we might be projecting our own cultural biases onto their system."

1235|

"Either way," Okafor said, "we need to figure out what the seven tunnels lead to. That's where the real answers are."

1236| 1237|

"That's coincidence," Okafor said, but his voice lacked conviction.

1238| 1239|

"Is it?" Elena turned to face him. "We landed on the Moon, crashed, breached a crater that had been sealed for millions of years, and now we're picking up a signal from the exact location where I found structures that look artificial and a symbol that matches the signal's pattern. How many coincidences does it take before you start looking for an explanation?"

1240| 1241|

1520|

"I'm not saying we abandon the module," Mensah said, her voice rising. "I'm saying we need a contingency plan. If the solar storm intensifies, if the radiation levels become lethal, we can't stay here. We need somewhere to go."

Instructions for AI coding assistants and developers working on the hermes-agent codebase.

## Development Environment

```bash
# Prefer .venv; fall back to venv if that's what your checkout has.
source .venv/bin/activate   # or: source venv/bin/activate
```

`scripts/run_tests.sh` probes `.venv` first, then `venv`, then
`$HOME/.hermes/hermes-agent/venv` (for worktrees that share a venv with the
main checkout).

```python
class AIAgent:

        api_mode: str = None,              # "chat_completions" | "codex_responses" | ...
        model: str = "",                   # empty → resolved from config/provider later

        enabled_toolsets: list = None,
        disabled_toolsets: list = None,
        quiet_mode: bool = False,
        save_trajectories: bool = False,
        platform: str = None,              # "cli", "telegram", etc.
        session_id: str = None,
        skip_context_files: bool = False,
        skip_memory: bool = False,
        credential_pool=None,
        # ... plus callbacks, thread/user/chat IDs, iteration_budget, fallback_model,
        # checkpoints config, prefill_messages, service_tier, reasoning_config, etc.
    ): ...

    def chat(self, message: str) -> str:
        """Simple interface — returns final response string."""

    def run_conversation(self, user_message: str, system_message: str = None,
                         conversation_history: list = None, task_id: str = None) -> dict:
        """Full interface — returns dict with final_response + messages."""
```

```python
            messages.append(tool_result_message(result))
        api_call_count += 1
    else:
```
